steps.text: **The question of this lesson.** The main line of the Declined looks like a long list of moves, but each move answers a threat or prepares a plan. By the end you can say what White's first seven moves are for, what Black's three answers to the bishop try to do, and step through two lines to about move fourteen and give a reason for every move. You will also see which alternatives the engine marks as mistakes, and why.

steps.text: **Black's three answers at move seven.** Our masters data lists 581 games here. Black simplifies with the knight jump to e4 (173 games, White scored 50%), builds with the pawn to b6 (274 games, 53%) or develops the queen's knight (124 games, 52%). [I] All three score close to half, which is why the line is called solid. Pick the plan by the job you want done.

**Plan A: trade pieces.** [H] A side with less room often improves by trading pieces, because the pieces that remain get more squares. The knight jump to e4 offers the first trade and also uncovers the bishop on e7, which now attacks the bishop on h4. White must answer at once. Our opening names call this the Lasker Defense (ECO D56) [V]. Step through the first two moves and see why.

steps.text: **Plan B: build, do not trade.** (Our opening names: the Tartakower Defense, ECO D58 [V].) The pawn move to b6 lets the bishop on c8 out on the long diagonal and keeps all the pieces for a later fight. It also changes what a capture on d5 means: after White takes, Black can retake with the knight, and then the bishop on h4 attacks the bishop on e7. Who gains from the trades that follow?

steps.text: **Three habits behind most mistakes here.** First, taking a piece while your own is attacked. Second, developing while a piece of yours is attacked more often than it is defended. Third, ignoring a capture the opponent has just made. All three come from skipping one question: what did my opponent's last move attack? The next three boards show the price.

steps.prompt: Teach it back. Imagine you teach a friend who knows how the pieces move. Write five sentences: (1) what the bishop on g5 attacks and why Black plays Be7, (2) what e3, Nf3, h6 and Bh4 are each for, (3) Black's three answers at move seven and the job of each, (4) one mistake and the question that avoids it, (5) one plan for each side in the Lasker structure and the Tartakower structure.

steps.text: **Self-check.** Did you say why the knight on f6 matters (it guards d5)? Did you give the job of each of the three black answers: trade, build, develop? Did you name one mistake and the question that avoids it (what did my opponent's last move attack)? Did you say what the half-open c-file gives White in Plan B? If one answer is missing, set the position up on a board and say it aloud once more.

**What to remember.**
- The bishop on g5 attacks the knight that guards d5; the bishop on e7 ends the pin.
- White develops and protects d4; the pawn on h6 asks the bishop to decide.
- Black has three jobs: trade (knight to e4), build (pawn to b6), develop (knight to d7).
- Retake first, then count attackers on every piece you leave behind.
- The exchange on d5 gives White the c-file and Black the e-file.
